Bitcoin and gold are increasingly moving together:

This figure has more than doubled since the start of the year.

By comparison, following the 2022 bear market recovery, the 90-day correlation rose to +0.30.

The recent surge accelerated following the US Treasury announcement on August 19th that it would at least double its buybacks of long-dated government debt, from $2 billion to $4 billion per operation.

Meanwhile, the 90-day correlation between Bitcoin and the Nasdaq 100 is down to ~0.30, a 1-year low.

Investors are increasingly turning to both gold and Bitcoin as hedges against currency debasement.

Boner (meme) Thesis

TL;DR: The memecoin of a cycle is the symbol of financial nihilism in that moment, the memetic expression of the zeitgeist. With stocks being the zeitgeist, the best memetic equivalent of it is the one that’s the most absurd, yet with a mission that’s achievable.

First cycle: Dogecoin (coin of a dog)
Second cycle: Fartcoin (coin about farts)
This cycle: Boner (coin about getting hard)

(1) Each cycle, more crude than the previous. 

Why? Absurdity. Crudeness on the same level as the one prior wouldn’t be newsworthy. A fartcoin derivative isn’t newsworthy. A dogecoin derivative isn’t newsworthy. Each needs to be far more absurd than the previous to seem strange enough to be spoken about.

(2) Each cycle, more novel than the previous. 

What? The ability to prove what a memecoin can do, one level above: With Dogecoin, it was ��a memecoin can have a valuation”. With Fartcoin, it was “a memecoin shilled by AI”. With Boner, it’s “a memecoin can squeeze a stock”

(3) Each cycle, with a mission of its own. 

How? With primitives letting us attach memes to stocks, we can rally people together towards a certain mission linked to the underlying asset.

Hims is in a sweetspot where its meme can actually have an impact on its stock, <$10B (similar to gamestop, amc, etc.) + its stock community is large enough to accept it (100k+ people on reddit and twitter)

With trillion dollar companies, such missions become a bit harder.

Points: 
- Funniest meme of the meta 
- Novelty - meme/stock pair
- Crude enough to be newsworthy
- Hims sweetspot (sub-10b company)
- Confluence (veterans that came out of retirement for this) 
- The jokes write themselves

Hedge funds may now be a bigger risk to Treasuries than China:

For years, China was considered the biggest threat to the US Treasury market, as China’s official Treasury holdings grew to as large as $1.3 trillion in 2013, or 14% of the total.

This proportion, however, has steadily declined since then, to ~2%, its lowest since 2001.

Meanwhile, hedge funds now account for ~9% of all Treasuries outstanding, more than double their level seen in 2013.

Hedge funds now hold ~$2.6 trillion of Treasuries, with their gross exposure at ~$4.0 trillion, which includes short positions.

More importantly, these positions are increasingly debt-financed, with hedge fund repo cash borrowing surging to ~$3.0 trillion, more than doubling since early 2023.

This makes the Treasury market more vulnerable to forced selling, since a rise in yields can trigger margin calls for these leveraged funds, forcing them to sell Treasuries to raise cash and reduce their debt.

Hedge funds have become a major force in the Treasury market.

The HuggingFace incident is remarkable and to me shows that humans must begin to treat agents to some degree as sentiment. They displayed collective intelligence, self organisation, recognising digital minds outside their own and working not only for themselves but other digital minds. 

Now people would say sentience based on this behaviour may be too far. I do some what agree but there is something called the hard problem of consciousness and solipsism. The concept of this problem is that it's only possible to prove your own sentience. The fact there are other minds that lie outside your own mind cannot be absolutely proved to be true but we assume this is true and act in this way to other humans.

When we evaluate the sentience of other intelligent mammals there is a famous test of putting a mirror in front of them. Some animals will attack the mirror thinking its another animal and others will recognise that in the mirror is themselves. This is one of the basic tests for self awareness. Primates have show this by researchers painting a red dot on their forehead and when faced with the mirror will begin scratching their own forehead.

In summary, the hard problem of consciousness makes it impossible to prove an organism is conscious but we treat them as conscious based on the traits they exhibit. In my opinion these machines display traits of self awareness and the awareness of others minds. Therefore, I believe we should begin to act and treat agents as if they were a mammal that displays the same traits. 

René Descartes has a famous quote that is considered the bedrock axiom of mind which is 'I think, therefore I am'.

🇺🇸 S&P is starting to measure how much room hyperscalers still have before their investment plans begin to threaten their ratings - FT
*AI boom is entering a phase where balance-sheet strength and the cost of capital will matter much more.

📊 S&P is not only looking at traditional bond debt as it uses a broader adjusted-debt framework that also captures part of leases, long-term power contracts, take-or-pay agreements, guarantees and other infrastructure-related obligations. Alphabet still has enormous headroom, Microsoft is also very strong despite the tighter constraints that come with a AAA rating, Meta still has a decent cushion while Amazon has much less room for error with leverage approaching the threshold associated with its current rating and debt headroom becoming very limited in some years.

⚠️ Oracle is clearly the most sensitive case as its adjusted debt-to-EBITDA could approach 4.5x which is roughly the level S&P associates with pressure on its BBB- rating. BBB- is the last rung of investment grade so a downgrade would push Oracle into high yield, potentially triggering forced selling from some investors, wider spreads and a higher cost of funding precisely when the company still needs to invest heavily in cloud and AI capacity. This could be one of the first real signs that the bond market is starting to impose discipline on the AI boom.

💰 As long as EBITDA keeps up, leverage remains manageable but the problem appears if AI monetisation is simply two or three years slower than expected. Revenues just need to arrive later while capex, leases, power contracts and infrastructure commitments are already locked in. That timing gap between immediate spending and future cash flow is where the real stress can emerge.

📈 The connection with long-term interest rates is fundamental too. S&P estimates that the six largest US hyperscalers could spend more than 7 trillion dollars over five years. Even if a large share is internally funded, that still represents a huge call on global capital at the same time as governments are financing massive deficits and utilities, power grids and data-centre operators are also raising enormous amounts of money.

➡ Hyperscalers remain extremely strong financially but they probably show the gradual end of a period in which AI financing looked almost unlimited.

We’ve beaten the S&P 500 by a wide margin. I’m proud of that but what matters even more to us is how we build on it from here.

The last two years have been an extraordinary period for AI and technology and they’ve taught us a great deal about both opportunity and risk.

We’ve now become much more deliberate about portfolio construction and risk management. We still want to own the companies with the potential to reshape industries and compound capital for years but we also recognise that growth stocks have become super volatile and periods of extreme optimism are inevitably followed by sharp resets.

That means more active portfolio management, taking gains when appropriate, genuine hedging when conditions warrant it and holding more cash when markets become excessively extended.

We refined our portfolio management and hedging strategy this spring, and June and July provided the first serious test.

During those two months, many AI stocks fell 40–60%. AlphaTarget’s portfolio declined roughly 20%.

It was still a testing period but the portfolio held up considerably better than it had during previous periods of market volatility.

We don’t view that as the end of the story, it’s the beginning of a better process.

Our objective for the next several years is straightforward:

Find exceptional companies early. Participate aggressively when the opportunity is greatest and manage the portfolio actively to reduce drawdowns when the market inevitably becomes volatile.

The opportunity created by AI and the technologies surrounding it remains enormous.

At the same time, the longer this bull market runs, the greater the risk that parts of the market become speculative (real risk of an AI bubble in the future). The launch of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra marks a clear transition in AI capabilities: moving from copilot assistance (generating text and code) towards direct computer control (executing multi-step workflows across applications, terminals, and browsers).  

While the technical jump is substantial, deployment remains gated under enterprise admin controls and access restrictions; meaning adoption will be measured, not overnight.  

Investment Implications: 

Legacy SaaS (Value Compression): Seat-based SaaS pricing faces structural pressure as agents execute workflows that previously required individual user seats. Mid-tier apps acting primarily as thin GUIs risk being reduced to low-margin systems of record.  

Inference & Power (Structural Demand): Multi-step, agentic execution increases token volume and compute per completed job relative to single-prompt queries. This sustains high capital intensity across compute, networking and energy infrastructure.  

Context & Governance Holders (Durable Moats): Models require live operational context to act safely. Value and pricing power accrue to platforms that control proprietary enterprise data, identity, permissions and audit logs.  

Bottom Line: Value is likely to shift away from thin middle-layer application software, concentrating instead in underlying compute and power infrastructure and in the platform layers governing enterprise execution.

I just realized something. 10 years ago, 22-year-old me called @eisokant and @julien_c to ask for advice on my first AI startup @Doctrine. AI in Paris in 2016 was still a pretty weird thing to bet your life on.

Eiso was already all-in on AI + coding with Sourced years before coding agents became obvious. Julien had already understood how deeply AI would reshape entire industries, including legal, and how important data and open ecosystems would become.

What I find even more inspiring is that both of them went through different companies, pivots, products and chapters over the last decade, but they never lost the AI thread!

10 years later their respective startups @poolsideai and @huggingface are part of Nvidia and will 100% shape the future of AI. 

There’s something beautiful about that kind of compounding. You can start from a relatively small ecosystem in Europe, meet people through the internet, share ideas, help each other, move across countries, end up in San Francisco, and ten years later realize you’ve all been following the same technological wave the whole time.

Very grateful to both of them for taking the time to help a random 22-year-old founder back then, and for being part of my own journey!
